noodles.notes: Flat-cut noodles (平打ち麺) developed jointly with the Nagoya ramen shop 俺の豚骨 (Ore no Tonkotsu) rather than made in-house — mochi-mochi springy, cut wide so a thin soup has surface to cling to. This is the one part of the bowl a specialist touched, and it shows: the body of the ramen is more serious than its soul. Hydration and maker are unpublished.

ramen.signature_bowl: 中華そば (chuka soba, ¥990) — pale soy soup with じんわりとした優しい旨味, a savouriness that arrives slowly rather than hitting, over wide flat noodles and dressed in the full Showa uniform: chashu, menma, negi, narutomaki, nori. It is not the house flagship. Noma-san built the shop around 町中華オムライス (¥1,320) — town-Chinese omurice — and the chuka soba is its noodle counterpart on a deliberately short opening menu, with more dishes promised as the kitchen finds its feet.
ramen.chashu: Sliced pork chashu in the plain machi-chuka manner — braised, thin-cut, laid flat over the noodles as one element among five rather than the centrepiece. The shop has published nothing about the cut or the braise and no reviewer has pressed the point; in this genre the chashu is expected to be modest, and it is.

gf.note: Wheat noodles and a wheat-brewed soy tare; no gluten-free option and no allergen protocol in a 12-seat shared-wok kitchen.

vegan.note: Animal stock, pork chashu, and a shared wok line. No plant-based bowl.

ramen.pantheon: This is the humblest register in ramen — the 中華そば of a 町中華, the soup a Chinese-restaurant cook ladles out between orders of fried rice, and the bowl a generation of Nagoya office workers grew up eating without ever calling it ramen. Noma-san came to cooking at forty after a career selling electrical equipment, trained around Nagoya's Chinese kitchens, and what he opened in December 2025 is that unglamorous lineage played completely straight: no oil cap, no fashion, nothing to prove, just a gently sweet soy broth and the naruto-and-nori dress code that dates the style to the Showa era. The soul is undemonstrative on purpose — machi-chuka soup is meant to be drinkable at the end of a shift, not stared at. Note that the kitchen has published nothing about its stock, so the chicken-chintan reading here is inference from tasting notes, not fact.

name: からめ亭 丸の内店 (Karametei Marunouchi)
reason: Ankake spaghetti specialist — fat spaghetti under a spiced tomato-Worcestershire gravy; no ramen, tsukemen or mazesoba on the menu.

name: 濃厚中華そば 佐とう (Noko Chuka Soba Sato)

noodles.notes: Medium-thin straight noodles with a hard, snapping bite — reviewers reach for ポキポキ, the word for something that breaks rather than yields. That is a low-hydration cut doing exactly the job it should: a soup this concentrated will invade any noodle that lets it in, so this one is built dry and stiff and stays defined to the last mouthful. Maker unpublished; the shop makes no jikasei-men claim.

ramen.signature_bowl: 濃厚中華そば (roughly ¥830–930) — a near-black bowl of tamari-soy broth carrying seafood umami and a heavy slick of scorched garlic oil, under a fan of paper-thin pork belly that covers the entire surface. The menu is deliberately tiny and the presentation austere: chashu, thick-cut white negi, nothing else. Kombu vinegar and black pepper sit on the tables, and by the halfway mark you will want them — the vinegar is the intended release valve, not an afterthought.
ramen.chashu: Pork belly, braised soft and shaved so thin it drapes, then piled in enough slices to hide the noodles entirely. This is the shop's inheritance made visible: before the pivot to ramen in October 2018 the owner ran a donburi restaurant, Le Granbowl, at the same address, and the meat handling came with him. The trick is volume without weight — it reads like an extravagant amount of pork and eats light because no single slice has any thickness to it.
notable_toppings: thin-sliced pork belly chashu, piled to cover the bowl
paper aprons handed out on request

gf.note: Wheat noodles. The tare is tamari shoyu, which in Aichi is soybean-dominant, but the shop makes no gluten-free claim and the noodles rule the bowl out regardless.

vegan.note: Pork belly chashu over a seafood-and-animal stock; nothing plant-based on the menu.

ramen.pantheon: The soul of this bowl is Aichi's own soy sauce. Tamari — thick, almost black, brewed from soybeans with little or no wheat, the condiment that makes Tokai cooking taste like Tokai — is normally used as a finishing dab on sashimi, and Sato builds an entire ramen on it, taking Nakagawa Jozo's tamari and refusing to blend it into politeness. What arrives looks like engine oil and drinks far easier than it looks: seafood umami underneath, a bitter-edged burnt-garlic oil floating on top, a tare concentrated enough that the shop keeps paper aprons behind the counter. Not every palate survives it — one careful reviewer found the garlic one-dimensional by the bottom of the bowl — and the honest reading is that this is a bowl with a single enormous idea rather than a balanced one. That is also why there is a queue outside a Marunouchi office block at 11am, six years running.

noodles.notes: Thin straight noodles are the house default and the thing regulars single out first — 細麺 is a Kyushu instinct and something of an outlier in Nagoya, where thicker cuts dominate. A medium gauge can be requested instead. Supplier and hydration undocumented.

ramen.signature_bowl: 楽いち味 ("the Rakuichi flavour", roughly ¥800–1,000) — the house pork-bone bowl, lifted by shima-tougarashi, the small fierce island chili of Okinawa, rather than by fat. Extra negi and a spoonful of kara-miso are the standard modifications; most regulars pair it with the chashu-don or the minced-pork rice as a set, sometimes for ¥50 off. Ten counter seats, one man cooking, evenings belong to regulars ordering beer alongside the bowl.
ramen.chashu: Pork chashu, tender and generously cut, doing double duty as the topping for the shop's chashu-don. It is the reason the rice sets sell: the same meat that sits on the noodles is what people come back for on rice. The shop publishes nothing about the cut or whether it is braised or seared.

gf.note: Wheat noodles and a wheat-brewed soy tare; no gluten-free noodle and no allergen policy at a one-man counter.

vegan.note: Pork-bone broth, pork chashu, pork rice sides. Nothing plant-based.

ramen.pantheon: A pork-bone bowl that refuses to be heavy. Tonkotsu's entire reputation rests on the violence of the boil — bones hammered for hours until fat and collagen emulsify into that opaque white soup — and Rakuichi keeps the pork soul while pulling the volume right down, to the point where regulars argue over whether it is あっさり or the made-up middle word こっさり: light on the tongue, still deep underneath. Anyone arriving expecting Hakata will find it thin; anyone tired of Hakata will find it exactly right. The heat is the shop's signature and it comes from chili, not fat — shima-tougarashi gives a dry, bright sting that lifts the pork instead of coating it, and the thin straight noodle is the correct body for a soup that never gets viscous. A residential side street near Meijo Park, ten seats, no press: the documentation is genuinely thin here and this reading should be treated as provisional.

name: 中華そば 白壁 あおい (Chuka Soba Shirakabe Aoi)

noodles.notes: 自家製中細縮れ麺 — house-made medium-thin crimped noodles, cut fresh daily. This is the Takayama signature and a genuine technical oddity: low-hydration dough (the style runs around 28–32%) is stiff and resists crimping, so almost nobody else in Japan makes a noodle both dry and strongly wavy. The point is twofold — the crimp gives a low-fat soup something to cling to, and the dry noodle then drinks that soup into itself, which is where the style's famous 一体感, soup-and-noodle-as-one-thing, comes from.

ramen.signature_bowl: 中華そば (roughly ¥800–900; the loaded 全部のせ around ¥1,000) — dark-looking soy broth that tastes nothing like it looks, over house-made crimped noodles, with pork chashu braised to collapse, thick crisp menma and a soft-centred ajitama. The first thing you get is a puff of katsuo, then vegetable sweetness. Miso soba (¥900), 焼豚そば (¥900) and a mazesoba (¥950) were added later, but the Takayama bowl is the shop's reason to exist; lunch comes with free rice, which locals use to mop the last of the broth.
ramen.chashu: Pork braised to the point of collapse — ホロっと, meaning it comes apart under the chopsticks rather than holding as a slice. That softness is deliberate against a soup carrying almost no fat of its own: the chashu supplies the richness the broth declines to. A dedicated 焼豚そば is on the menu for anyone who wants the meat to lead the bowl instead of supporting it.
notable_toppings: thick-cut menma, assertively seasoned yet soft
ajitsuke tamago with a silky yolk

gf.note: Wheat noodles, and the wheat-brewed soy tare is boiled through the whole stockpot — there is no unseasoned soup here at all.

vegan.note: Chicken, pork and beef stock with a katsuo dashi note, plus pork chashu and a marinated egg.

ramen.pantheon: A Hida-Takayama bowl transplanted 150km south, and one of Japan's genuine structural oddities. Everywhere else in ramen, broth and tare are kept apart on purpose, so one pot of soup can yield shoyu, shio or miso by swapping the seasoning at the last second. Takayama refuses the split: the soy tare goes into the zundo and simmers with the stock, which is why Hida chuka soba comes in exactly one flavour and can never come in another. What that produces is a soup that looks dark and reads gentle — chicken and pork bones with beef and a heap of aromatic onion, a bonito lift on the first sip, almost no fat on the surface, a sweetness that is vegetable rather than sugared. A low-fat soup should feel thin, and this one does not, because the body rescues it: dry, strongly crimped noodles that grip the broth and then absorb it. Ryuichiro Sawa inherited this counter from his parents at 35 and went on to build the 59-shop Fujiyama 55 tsukemen chain out of it — the empire is elsewhere, but the family recipe, and the repeated pilgrimages he made up to Takayama to get it honest, are here.

noodles.notes: Thin noodles chosen for のどごし — the slippery throat-feel that a low-oil salt broth wants, since there is no fat to carry the noodle down. Cut, hydration and maker are unpublished.

ramen.signature_bowl: 鶏レモンラーメン (chicken lemon ramen, ¥870) — a clear chicken-and-salt soup laid with overlapping lemon slices and a nest of shiraga-negi, with chicken chashu in place of pork so the whole bowl stays on one animal and nothing muddies the citrus. The oil content is low enough that regulars finish the soup without guilt. The counter runs two stocks side by side, the chicken chuka-soba base and a tonkotsu, so the same twenty-seat room serves the brightest bowl in the neighbourhood and its opposite; gyoza and chashu-don fill out the sides, and lunch sets come with rice and pickles.
ramen.chashu: Chicken chashu, not pork — cooked until it crumbles at the touch of the chopsticks, lean and seasoned lightly so it never fights the lemon. Choosing bird over pig here is a structural decision, not a health one: pork fat and citrus argue, and the bowl is built to keep them apart. The tonkotsu side of the menu reverts to conventional pork chashu.
notable_toppings: sliced lemon laid across the surface
gyoza and chashu rice bowls alongside
lunch sets with rice and pickles

gf.note: Wheat noodles, a soy-and-dashi based tare, and gyoza wrappers in a small shared kitchen. No gluten-free option.

vegan.note: Both house stocks are animal — chicken bone and pork bone — and the bowl is finished with chicken chashu.

ramen.pantheon: Lemon ramen is a recent Japanese fashion rather than an inherited regional style, and it earns its place by inverting the usual method: instead of building depth out of fat, it strips the oil away and lets acid and aroma do the carrying. The soul is a clear chicken chintan under a shio tare — the most exposed construction in all of ramen, because there is no fat cap and no dark soy to hide behind, and a stock that is anything less than clean will announce itself immediately. Here it holds. The lemon perfumes every lift of the noodles rather than souring the soup, the shiraga-negi adds a raw allium edge, and the chicken chashu keeps the bowl monochrome in the best sense. Open since June 2013 on a quiet Higashi-ku street, with the tonkotsu pot waiting on the other side of the menu for the nights when you want the exact opposite.

name: あんかけ太郎 名古屋城金シャチ横丁店 (Ankake Taro Nagoya Castle Kinshachi Yokocho)
reason: Single-dish ankake spaghetti operator — fat spaghetti under a spiced tomato-Worcestershire gravy; no ramen, tsukemen or mazesoba served.

name: 柳城 NAGOYA CASTLE (Ryujo Nagoya Castle)
reason: Cantonese fine-dining room in the Espacio Nagoya Castle hotel — courses, dim sum and crispy pork; its only noodle offerings are chilled hiyashi-chuka/reimen course swaps, not ramen.

name: LIT（リト） (LIT (Rito))
reason: Ankake pasta shop grown out of a spice-curry cafe and food truck; serves Nagoya ankake spaghetti, not ramen.
